# Introduction

## Introduction

In the following presentation our idea is to share the way the Density Matrix (DM) model works, using it for a real case study.

## Case study - Palmer Penguins

We will be working with the Palmer `penguins` dataset, which is a well-known dataset in the R community for classification tasks. The goal is to classify penguin species based on various features. The `penguins` dataset is as follows:

```{r DM-1, echo=FALSE}
Data <- modeldata::penguins
Data %>% glimpse()
```

## Case study - Palmer Penguins

Our objective, therefore, is to identify the species using all the other variables as predictors. The species are Adelie, Chinstrap, and Gentoo.

<img src="https://allisonhorst.github.io/palmerpenguins/reference/figures/lter_penguins.png" width="600px"/>

# Data preparation

## Data preparation - Species selection

However, due to the limitations of our model so far, we will be working with only 2 of those species: Adelie and Gentoo, the ones whose difference in `Body mass` and `Flipper length` can allow us to separate them more easily.

```{r DM-2 }
Data %<>% 
  filter(species != "Chinstrap") %>%
  mutate(y = ifelse(species == "Adelie", "0", "1"), .keep = "unused") %>%
  mutate(y = factor(y)) %>% 
  relocate(y)
```

## Data preparation - aNAlysis

We will just drop the `NA` values.

```{r DM-3 }
Data %<>% na.omit()
```

## Data preparation - Number of Categories

```{r DM-4, echo = FALSE}
qml::plot_n_levels(Data)
```

## Data preparation - split

For the sake of comparison, we will split the data into a training set and a test set, using a proportion defined in the parameters section. We will stratify the split based on the `species` variable to ensure that both species are represented proportionally in both sets.

```{r DM-6 }
Data_split <- Data %>% rsample::initial_split(prop = 1 - params$test_prop, strata = "y")
Data_train <- Data_split %>% rsample::training()
Data_test <- Data_split %>% rsample::testing()
```


# The DM workflow

## DM - Modern tidymodels Interface

The qml package now follows tidymodels conventions with a modern `dm_fit()` and `predict()` interface. This separates model fitting from prediction and follows established R modeling patterns.

**Key functions:**
- `dm_fit()`: Fits the quantum matrix classifier
- `predict()`: Makes predictions on new data
- Supporting functions for visualization and analysis

The new interface is more robust and follows tidymodels standards.

## DM - K (Kernel function)

The function `K` defines the kernel used in `f_hat_h` for smooth density estimation around points. It operates on differences scaled by the window bandwidth.

**Usage example:**

```{r DM-9, warning=FALSE}
library(ggplot2)
# Kernel function at a vector point c(0.1, 0.2)
v <- (-110:110)/100
expand.grid(x = v, y = v) %>%
  mutate(z = purrr::pmap_dbl(select(., x, y), ~ K(c(...), r = 2))) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = x, y = y, z = z)) +
  geom_raster(aes(fill = z)) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c() +
  labs(title = "Kernel Function K(x)", x = "x", y = "y", fill = "K(x)") +
  theme_minimal()
```

**Mathematical definition:**

\[
K(x) = 
\begin{cases}
\frac{1}{2} (r+2)(1 - \|x\|^2) & \text{if } \|x\|^2 < 1 \\
0 & \text{otherwise}
\end{cases}
\]

where \(r\) is the dimension (default 2), and \(\|x\|^2 = \sum_i x_i^2\).

## DM - Model Fitting

The `dm_fit()` function fits the quantum matrix classifier using tidymodels conventions. It processes the dataset, creates quantum density matrices, and stores all necessary information for prediction.

**Usage example:**

```{r DM-10}
# Fit the quantum matrix classifier
dm_model <- dm_fit(y ~ ., data = Data_train, n_breaks = 3)
print(dm_model)
```

## DM - Model fitting

**Key features:**
- Follows R modeling conventions with formula interface
- Stores preprocessing parameters for consistent predictions
- Returns a fitted model object with summary information

**Mathematical concept:**

The quantum density matrix \(\rho_d = \frac{X X^\top}{\text{trace}(X X^\top)}\) represents class covariances in a quantum-inspired manner.

## DM - Predictions

The `predict()` method makes predictions using the fitted quantum matrix classifier. It supports both class predictions and probability estimates.

## DM - Predictions

```{r DM-11, warning=FALSE}
# Class predictions
class_pred <- predict(dm_model, newdata = Data_test)
table(class_pred)
```

## DM - Predictions

```{r DM-12, warning=FALSE}
# Probability predictions  
prob_pred <- predict(dm_model, newdata = Data_test, type = "prob")
head(prob_pred)
```

## DM - Predictions

**Key features:**
- Standard `predict()` interface following R conventions
- Supports `type = "class"` and `type = "prob"`
- Uses stored preprocessing parameters for consistent transformation
- Returns standard factor/tibble formats

**Coordinate conversion:**

Internally converts to polar coordinates: \(r = \sqrt{V_1^2 + V_2^2}, \phi_1 = \tan^{-1}(V_2/V_1)\)

## DM - Model Summary and Diagnostics

The fitted model provides comprehensive information about the training process and model characteristics.

**Usage example:**

```{r DM-14}
# Model summary
summary(dm_model)
```

**Available information:**
- Training data statistics
- Class distributions in polar coordinates  
- Preprocessing parameters
- Model performance metrics

**Mathematical foundation:**

Kernel density estimation: \(\hat{f}_h(x|e_y) = \sum_{\tilde{X} \in \tilde{\chi}_{r, e_y}} \frac{1}{n h^r} K\left(\frac{x - \tilde{X}_r}{h}\right)\)

where \( \tilde{\chi}_{r, e_y} \) are the surrogate training vectors for class \( e_y \).

## DM - Complete Workflow

The complete quantum matrix workflow now follows modern R practices with clean separation of concerns.

**Complete usage example:**

```{r DM-15, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
# Fit the model
dm_model <- dm_fit(y ~ ., data = Data_train, n_breaks = 3)

# Make predictions
predictions <- predict(dm_model, newdata = Data_test)
probabilities <- predict(dm_model, newdata = Data_test, type = "prob")

# Combine results for analysis
result <- Data_test %>%
  mutate(
    .pred = predictions,
    .truth = y
  ) %>%
  bind_cols(probabilities) %>%
  # Add polar coordinates for visualization (if needed)
  select(.pred, .truth, everything())

head(result)
```

This approach is more robust, follows tidymodels conventions, and separates model fitting from prediction.

# Visualization

## Visualization

Our result is a tibble with predictions, probabilities, and true classes. For visualization purposes, we can extract the polar coordinates if needed.

```{r DM-16, echo=TRUE}
result %>% head
```

**Key advantages of the new approach:**
- Clean separation between model fitting and prediction
- Follows established R modeling conventions
- More robust error handling and validation
- Consistent with tidymodels ecosystem
- Better integration with other R packages

## Visualization - Classification Results

```{r DM-17, echo=FALSE}
# Simple visualization of classification results
result %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = .pred, fill = .truth)) +
  geom_bar(position = "dodge", alpha = 0.8) +
  labs(
    title = "Classification Results",
    x = "Predicted Class", 
    y = "Count",
    fill = "True Class"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

## Metrics

```{r DM-18, echo=FALSE}
library(yardstick)
my_metrics = metric_set(bal_accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, ppv, npv, accuracy, f_meas, kap, mcc)
my_metrics(result, truth = .truth, estimate = .pred)
```

## Probability Analysis

We can analyze the prediction probabilities to understand model confidence:

```{r DM-19, echo=FALSE}
# Analyze prediction probabilities
result %>%
  select(starts_with(".pred_"), .truth) %>%
  tidyr::pivot_longer(cols = starts_with(".pred_"), 
               names_to = "predicted_class", 
               values_to = "probability") %>%
  mutate(predicted_class = stringr::str_remove(predicted_class, ".pred_")) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = probability, fill = predicted_class)) +
  # geom_histogram(alpha = 0.7, bins = 20) +
  geom_density(alpha = 0.7, bins = 20) +
  facet_wrap(~.truth, labeller = label_both) +
  labs(
    title = "Prediction Probability Distribution by True Class",
    x = "Predicted Probability",
    y = "Count",
    fill = "Predicted Class"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

## Model Performance Summary

```{r DM-20, echo=FALSE}
# Create a summary of model performance
performance_summary <- result %>%
  summarise(
    total_predictions = n(),
    correct_predictions = sum(.pred == .truth),
    accuracy = correct_predictions / total_predictions,
    class_0_precision = sum(.pred == "0" & .truth == "0") / sum(.pred == "0"),
    class_1_precision = sum(.pred == "1" & .truth == "1") / sum(.pred == "1"),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

performance_summary %>%
  tidyr::pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "metric", values_to = "value") %>%
  mutate(value = round(value, 3)) %>%
  knitr::kable(caption = "Model Performance Summary")
```

## Confusion matrix - Train vs Test

This table was generated for **one** split, without resampling.

```{r DM-22 }
result %>% select(.pred, .truth) %>% table()
```

# Notes

## Key Improvements

**Modern Implementation Benefits:**
- **Tidymodels Integration**: Follows established R modeling conventions
- **Robust Error Handling**: Better validation and informative error messages  
- **Consistent Interface**: Standard `fit()` and `predict()` workflow
- **Reproducible Results**: Stored preprocessing parameters ensure consistency
- **Better Documentation**: Comprehensive help files and examples

## ML

- On `DMnML.Rmd` an extended DM model is included for **bootstrap resampling**.
- The new implementation is more suitable for integration with tidymodels workflows.
